name: Black-Eyed Children
description: A late-1990s internet-born paranormal legend describing encounters with apparently human children or teenagers whose eyes are entirely black, who appear unannounced at doors or vehicles, and who request entry in an unsettlingly insistent way.
full_description: Black-Eyed Children (BEK) are a contemporary paranormal phenomenon and internet-era folkloric figure. The modern legend was launched in January 1996 when Texan reporter Brian Bethel posted to a ghost-related mailing list a personal account of encountering two boys, aged about 9 and 12, with completely black eyes — sclera, iris, and pupil all jet black — who tried to persuade him to let them into his car outside a movie theatre in Abilene, Texas. Bethel's post mentioned a second, unrelated sighting reported from Portland, Oregon. The post circulated widely on the early web and inspired a steady stream of similar accounts from other witnesses, particularly through paranormal forums in the early 2000s. The figures are typically described as resembling normal children or teenagers, often pale-skinned, sometimes oddly dressed, who knock at doors or windows and ask insistently to be let in. Witnesses report a strong sense of unease, often well before the eye anomaly is noticed. Folklorists including Sharon A. Hill have analysed BEK accounts as friend-of-a-friend narratives following the contours of long-standing 'don't open the door' folklore. Snopes and similar fact-checking outlets categorise the phenomenon as legend rather than evidence.
origin: Reports concentrated in the United States (particularly Texas, the Pacific Northwest, and the Midwest), with later international reports in the United Kingdom, Australia, and elsewhere as the legend circulated online.

etymology.origin: Coined as a descriptive label in Brian Bethel's 1996 internet posts and 1998 'A Strange Encounter With Black-Eyed Kids' column.
etymology.meaning: Children or teenagers with completely black eyes — no visible whites, irises, or pupils.

timeline.event: Brian Bethel posts his Abilene, Texas, account to a ghost-related mailing list
timeline.significance: Birth of the modern BEK legend

timeline.event: Bethel publishes 'A Strange Encounter With Black-Eyed Kids' as a column
timeline.significance: Brings the story to a much wider audience

timeline.event: Bethel appears on the Discovery Channel series Monsters and Mysteries in America discussing his 1996 encounter
timeline.source: Monsters and Mysteries in America, season 1

timeline.event: MSN's Weekly Strange airs an episode on Black-Eyed Children reports
UK Daily Star runs three sensationalist front-page stories on Cannock Chase BEK reports
timeline.significance: Drives the second wave of public interest

timeline.event: Independent horror film Black Eyed Kids enters Kickstarter funding

cultural_notes: BEK belief is a feature of online paranormal subcultures; it has not penetrated mainstream institutional belief or practice.
